lines.text: Rainforest caves, a sultanate on a busy strait, tin, rubber and empire, then a young federation reaching for the sky. This is the story of Malaysia.
Some forty thousand years ago, people were already living in the great Niah Caves of Sarawak, on Borneo.
Around 1400 the Malacca Sultanate rose on the strait between the seas, a rich trading port that spread Islam across the region.
In 1511 the Portuguese took Malacca, the first of the European powers to arrive. The Dutch would follow.
Then came the British. Under their rule, tin mines and rubber estates made fortunes and drew workers from China and India.
In the 1850s a tin-mining camp took root where two rivers meet. It grew into Kuala Lumpur, the capital.
Tunku Abdul Rahman, born a prince in 1903, would lead the country to freedom as its first prime minister.
Mahathir Mohamad, born in 1925, would lead the country for twenty-two years and turn it into an industrial nation.
Anwar Ibrahim, a reformer born in 1947, would be jailed twice before finally becoming prime minister.
In 1948 a long jungle war began against communist guerrillas, lasting twelve years.
On the thirty-first of August 1957, the Tunku proclaimed independence, still celebrated every year as Merdeka Day.
Indonesia opposed the plan for a wider federation and took up arms, a confrontation that lasted three years.
Even so, in 1963 an agreement joined Malaya, Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak together.
Malaysia was born, a federation with a rotating king chosen from among the sultans of its states.
Within two years Singapore left, and on the ninth of August 1965 it became independent on its own.
In May 1969, race riots shook Kuala Lumpur, and new policies favouring the Malays followed.
In 1974 the state oil company Petronas was founded, and oil became a pillar of the economy.
Lee Chong Wei, born in 1982, would become one of the great badminton players, world number one for nearly seven years.
In 1983 Mahathir's Malaysia founded Proton, its own national car maker.
From 1995 a planned city, Putrajaya, rose south of Kuala Lumpur as the new seat of government.
And in Kuala Lumpur the Petronas Towers, twin spires joined by a sky bridge, became for a time the tallest buildings in the world.
In 2009 a state fund called 1MDB was set up. Billions vanished from it, and former prime minister Najib Razak went to jail.
In 2014 Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 vanished with two hundred and thirty-nine people on board, a mystery that gripped the world.
In 2018 voters changed their government for the first time since independence, bringing back Mahathir at the age of ninety-two.
From cave dwellers to twin towers, Malaysia keeps building on its many peoples and its long trade.
